'''''The Quick and the Dead''''' is a 1995 American [[revisionist Western]] film directed by [[Sam Raimi]]. The film stars [[Sharon Stone]], [[Gene Hackman]], [[Russell Crowe]] and [[Leonardo DiCaprio]]. The screenplay was written by [[Simon Moore (writer)|Simon Moore]] but includes contributions from [[Joss Whedon]].<ref name=Whedon>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbr.com/sam-raimi-explains-why-spider-man-4-didnt-happen/|title=Sam Raimi Explains Why Spider-Man 4 Didn't Happen|work=Spinoff Online &#124; TV & Film News Daily |date=March 6, 2013|publisher=Spinoff Online|access-date=August 21, 2014|archive-date=August 21, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140821201913/http://spinoff.comicbookresources.com/2013/03/06/sam-raimi-explains-why-spider-man-4-didnt-happen/|url-status=live}}</ref> The story focuses on "The Lady" (Stone), a [[gunfighter]] who rides into the [[American frontier|frontier]] town of Redemption, controlled by John Herod (Hackman). The Lady joins a deadly dueling competition in an attempt to exact revenge for her father's death.

Simon Moore's script was purchased by [[Sony Pictures Entertainment]] in May 1993, and actress Sharon Stone signed on as both star and co-producer. Development was fast-tracked after director Sam Raimi's hiring, and [[principal photography]] began in [[Old Tucson Studios]] in [[Arizona]] on November 21, 1993. The film was distributed by [[TriStar Pictures]] and was released in the United States on February 10, 1995, to a [[box-office bomb|dismal box-office performance]], receiving mixed reviews from critics. In later years, however, the film earned critical praise, especially for the performances, direction, cinematography and musical score, with some critics noting it as underrated in Raimi's catalog.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2009/09/08/the-quick-and-the-dead-blu-ray-review |title=The Quick and the Dead Blu-ray Review - IGN |date=September 8, 2009 |access-date=May 3, 2019 |archive-date=May 3, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190503075847/https://www.ign.com/articles/2009/09/08/the-quick-and-the-dead-blu-ray-review |url-status=live |website=IGN}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.slashfilm.com/853138/sam-raimis-western-f-rules/ | title=Sam Raimi's Western F****** Rules | date=May 5, 2022 }}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine | url=https://ew.com/movies/sam-raimi-films-ranked/ | title=The films of Sam Raimi, ranked | magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] | access-date=November 9, 2022 | archive-date=November 9, 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221109111310/https://ew.com/movies/sam-raimi-films-ranked/ | url-status=live |last=Stenzel|first=Wesley|date=October 8, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://collider.com/sam-raimi-the-quick-and-the-dead-best-90s-western/ | title=This is the Best '90s Western That Isn't 'Unforgiven' | website=[[Collider (website)|Collider]] | date=May 3, 2023 |last=Williamson|first=Samuel}}</ref>

==Plot==
In 1881, a [[Gunfighter|gunslinger]] known as "The Lady" arrives in the [[American frontier|Old West]] town of Redemption, which is ruled by a ruthless outlaw-turned-mayor named John Herod. Herod has announced a fast-draw [[bracket (tournament)|single-elimination]] shooting tournament with a large cash prize for the winner. The rules stipulate that any contestant may challenge any other, no challenge can be refused, every contestant must fight once per day, and a fight continues until one contestant either yields or dies. The Lady announces her participation, insisting she is interested only in the prize.

During the sign-up, Herod's henchmen arrive with Cort, an exceptionally skilled gunfighter and a former member of their gang. Cort has renounced violence to become a [[preacher]] and refuses to participate in the tournament. Herod's men [[lynching|attempt to lynch him]], but The Lady shoots through the rope, freeing him. The Lady meets "The Kid", a brash young man who believes Herod is his father and hopes to earn his respect by winning the tournament. She wakes up alone in The Kid's bed and notices some barrels of loose [[dynamite]] under it. 

In the first round, Herod kills Ace Hanlon, a braggart who took credit for some of Herod's kills as an outlaw. The Kid and The Lady easily defeat their opponents. Herod buys a cheap gun for Cort from The Kid and declares he can have only one bullet at a time, to prevent him from shooting his way out of town. Despite his conversion, Cort reflexively draws when challenged and wins his first-round duel.

Before the second round, Herod meets with Clay Cantrell, a professional gunfighter hired by the townspeople to kill him. Herod declares all duels are now to the death and kills Cantrell. The Kid wins his second fight against Scars, an escaped convict. The Lady faces Eugene Dred after he molests the saloon owner's young daughter, eventually killing him. Upset, she rides out of town.

Meanwhile, Cort duels a Native American gunslinger, Spotted Horse, but fails to kill him with the first shot and succeeds with a second bullet thrown by a spectator. Doc Wallace finds The Lady at a nearby cemetery and tells her he recognizes her and knows why she is there. Flashbacks reveal that The Lady's real name is Ellen McKenzie. Her father was the [[marshal]] in Redemption until Herod's gang invaded and [[Lynching|lynched]] him. Herod gave Ellen a pistol and three shots to try to break the rope, but she accidentally killed her father, after which she fled town. Doc hands Ellen her father's old badge and persuades her to help rid the town of Herod.

The following day, Ellen challenges Herod, but he has already accepted a challenge from The Kid. As Ellen and Cort are the only fighters left, Herod orders them to fight, threatening to kill them if they refuse. Herod urges The Kid to withdraw, but he refuses. Although Herod is wounded, The Kid is fatally shot. Herod coldly refuses to take his hand as he dies, and says afterward it was never proven he was The Kid's father. When Cort and Ellen face off, Cort draws and fires on her, and Doc declares her dead. Cort angrily demands to fight Herod immediately, but he settles for dawn the next day. That night, Ratsy, one of Herod's men, breaks Cort's right hand. 

The next morning, Herod rebukes Ratsy and kills him for harming Cort. Herod confesses that he is afraid of Cort, which is why he forced him to enter the tournament. As a matter of honor, he offers to fight Cort left-handed, but still instructs his henchmen to kill Cort if he wins. At the moment Herod draws, several buildings explode, including Herod's house and the clock tower. Ellen emerges from the smoke and flames, having faked her death and planted The Kid's dynamite with help from Cort and Doc. Cort kills Herod's remaining henchmen while Ellen faces off against Herod, revealing her identity by throwing her father's badge at his feet. Herod wounds Ellen, but she shoots him through the chest and kills him with a bullet to the eye. She tosses the badge to Cort and rides away, leaving him in charge of bringing law and order to Redemption.

==Production==

===Development===
Writer Simon Moore finished his [[spec script|speculative script]] for ''The Quick and the Dead'' in late 1992, writing it as an [[Homage (arts)|''homage'']] to the [[spaghetti Western]]s of [[Sergio Leone]], particularly ''[[Once Upon a Time in the West]]'' and the ''[[Dollars Trilogy]]'' starring [[Clint Eastwood]]. The writer decided the lead character should be a female. "When you introduce women into that kind of world, something very interesting happens and you have an interesting dynamic straight away", Moore commented.<ref name=first/> The names of the lead villain ([[Herod the Great|Herod]]) and the town ([[Redemption (theology)|Redemption]]) were intentional allusions to [[Bible|the Bible]].<ref name=first/> Moore considered directing his own script as an [[independent film]] and shooting ''The Quick and the Dead'' on a $3–4&nbsp;million budget in either Spain or Italy.<ref name=first/>

[[Sony Pictures Entertainment]] purchased Moore's script in May 1993 and approached Sharon Stone, fresh off the success of ''[[Basic Instinct]]'', to star in the lead role in July 1993.<ref name=first>Muir, pp. 171-179</ref> Because Stone also signed on as co-producer, she had approval of the choice of director. Sam Raimi was hired to direct because Stone was impressed with his work on ''[[Army of Darkness]]'' (1992); she made it clear that if he was not hired, she would quit the project. Although Stone had mixed emotions on Raimi's previous work, she believed in his ability to handle the campy tone of the film, feeling that ''The Quick and the Dead'' would be a perfect opportunity to "stretch the limits of his technical and creative ability".<ref name="Comp">{{cite book | author = Warren | title = The Evil Dead Companion | year = 2000 | publisher = [[Titan Books]] | location = London | chapter = Blood Still in the Veins | pages = 162–179 | isbn = 0-312-27501-3|first=Bill|author-link=Bill Warren (film historian)}}</ref> Moore was also enthusiastic over Raimi's hiring based on his previous work with the [[The Evil Dead (franchise)|''Evil Dead'' film series]].<ref name=first/>

When Sony began [[wikt:Fast track|fast-tracking]] development of ''The Quick and the Dead,'' the studio commissioned a series of rewrites from Moore. The writer was eventually dismissed and replaced with [[John Sayles]], who, according to Moore, was chosen because the studio did not like the semi-serious tone and instructed him toward "making more of an [[American Old West]] film".<ref name=second/> Moore was rehired and filming was to begin in three weeks because Sayles's script was approaching a 2½-hour runtime. When rewriting the [[shooting script]], Moore omitted Sayles's work without Sony noticing. A week before shooting, Sony considered the script good enough to shoot; Moore described the rewrites as "a completely fucking pointless exercise".<ref name=second/>

===Filming===
Russell Crowe originally auditioned for a different role in the film before Sharon Stone asked that the actor try for the lead male role. "When I saw ''[[Romper Stomper]]'' [1992], I thought Russell was not only charismatic, attractive and talented, but also fearless", Stone reasoned. "And I find fearlessness very attractive. I was convinced I wouldn't scare him."<ref name=new/> Raimi found Crowe to be "bold and challenging. He reminds me of what we imagine the American cowboy to have been like."<ref name="new">{{cite news | author = Diamond | title = Straight Out of Australia, to L.A. | work = [[The New York Times]] | date = March 26, 1995 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/03/26/movies/straight-out-of-australia-to-la.html|first=Jamie|page=24}}</ref> On working with Raimi, Crowe later described the director as "sort of like the fourth [[The Three Stooges|Stooge]]".<ref name=first/>

[[Image:Sam Raimi by David Shankbone.jpg|thumb|145px|left|Director Sam Raimi]]
Sony Pictures had doubts with Stone's choice of Crowe because he was unknown to American audiences in the mid-1990s.<ref name=first/> To cast Gene Hackman in the role of Herod, TriStar Pictures changed the shooting location from [[Durango]], Mexico, to [[Tucson, Arizona|Tucson]], Arizona.<ref>{{cite news | author = Archerd | url = https://variety.com/1993/voices/columns/douglas-wows-greedy-cast-crew-1117862241/ | title = Douglas wows 'Greedy' cast, crew | date = August 16, 1993 | work = [[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] | access-date = March 7, 2009 | archive-date = October 25, 2012 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121025150043/http://www.variety.com/article/VR1117862241 | url-status = live |first=Army|author-link=Army Archerd}}</ref> [[Matt Damon]] was offered the role of Fee "The Kid" Herod, but declined.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=s6ZbAgAAQBAJ&q=matt+damon+quick+and+the+dead&pg=PT27|title=Matt Damon|isbn=9781438141220|last1=Woog|first1=Adam|year=2012|publisher=Infobase Learning }}</ref> [[Sam Rockwell]] also auditioned for The Kid, a role that ended up going to Leonardo DiCaprio.<ref>{{cite news | author = Rebecca Murray; Fred Topel | url = http://movies.about.com/library/weekly/aaconfessionsintb.htm | title = Sam Rockwell Talks About ''Confessions of a Dangerous Mind'' | work = [[About.com]] | access-date = March 7, 2009 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090227215636/http://movies.about.com/library/weekly/aaconfessionsintb.htm | archive-date = February 27, 2009 }}</ref> Sony was also hesitant about the inexperienced DiCaprio's casting; Stone compromised by paying his salary out of her own pocket.<ref name=first/>

Filming was originally to begin in October 1993<ref name=film/> but was delayed because Crowe needed to finish a prior commitment in Australia.<ref name=first/> [[Principal photography]] for ''The Quick and the Dead'' lasted from November 21, 1993, to February 27, 1994.<ref name="film">{{cite news | author = Archerd | url = https://variety.com/1993/voices/columns/lemmon-enjoying-fruitful-outings-1117862363/ | title = Lemmon enjoying fruitful outings | date = October 13, 1993 | work = [[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] | access-date = March 7, 2009 | archive-date = October 25, 2012 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121025150107/http://www.variety.com/article/VR1117862363 | url-status = live |first=Army}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | author = Archerd | url = https://variety.com/1994/voices/columns/friends-stunned-saddened-by-shore-s-death-1117862435/ | title = Friends stunned, saddened by Shore's death | date = February 25, 1994 | work = [[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] | access-date = March 7, 2009 | archive-date = October 25, 2012 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121025150135/http://www.variety.com/article/VR1117862435 | url-status = live |first=Army}}</ref> Locations included [[Old Tucson Studios]] in Arizona<ref name=first/> and [[Mescal, Arizona|Mescal]], {{convert|40|miles}} southeast of Tucson.<ref name=second/> Production was briefly halted at times over weather problems.<ref name=third/> [[Thell Reed (Shooter)|Thell Reed]], who was hired as the gun coach and [[weapons master]],<ref name=first/> worked with the cast during three months of training.<ref name=second/> To age Cort's [[Colt 1851 Navy Revolver]] and the other guns used, Reed experimented with simple measures. "I took them out by my swimming pool and dipped them in chlorine water to let them rust", he explained. "They looked rusty and old, but were brand new guns."<ref name=third/> Such detail, including the [[nickel]] plating and ivory handles on Ellen's [[Colt Single Action Army|Colt Peacemakers]], was accurate to the time period.<ref name=third>Muir, pp.190-197</ref>

The town of Redemption was designed by [[Patrizia von Brandenstein]], known for her work on ''[[Amadeus (film)|Amadeus]]'' (1984) and ''[[The Untouchables (film)|The Untouchables]]'' (1987).<ref name=second/> Raimi's first choice as the [[visual effects supervisor]] was [[Flash Film Works|William Mesa]], his collaborator on ''[[Darkman]]'' (1990) and ''[[Army of Darkness]]'' (1992). Instead, Sony chose [[Framestore|The Computer Film Company]] to create the VFX sequences.<ref name=first/> [[Pick-up (filmmaking)|Pick-up]] scenes took place in November and December 1994, including an extended duel between Sharon Stone and Gene Hackman.<ref>{{cite news | author = Archerd | url = https://variety.com/1994/voices/columns/h-w-d-pumped-for-sequel-to-gump-1117862606/ | title = H'w'd pumped for sequel to 'Gump' | date = December 20, 1994 | work = [[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] | access-date = March 7, 2009 | archive-date = October 25, 2012 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121025150226/http://www.variety.com/article/VR1117862606 | url-status = live |first=Army}}</ref>

Stone had a love scene with Crowe removed from the final cut before the film's release in the United States.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Ck9WAAAAIBAJ&pg=6765,2873726&dq=quick-and-the-dead+stone&hl=en |title=Winnie Mandela Caught in New Flap|publisher=Eugene Register-Guard|access-date=February 19, 2011|date= February 12, 1995 |via=Google News}}</ref> The actress/co-producer thought the scene did not fit with the picture's established reality.<ref name=second/> It was included in overseas releases of the film, both theatrically and on home media.

===Soundtrack===
The original motion-picture [[Soundtrack album|soundtrack]] for ''The Quick and the Dead'' was released by the [[Varèse Sarabande]] music label on February 14, 1995.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0000014WE |title=The Quick and the Dead Soundtrack |website=Amazon |year=1995 |access-date=April 10, 2011 |archive-date=July 1, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210701005250/https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0000014WE |url-status=live }}</ref> The score for the film was composed and conducted by [[Alan Silvestri]] and mixed by [[Dennis S. Sands|Dennis Sands]]. Kenneth Karman and Thomas Drescher edited the film's music.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://movies.yahoo.com/movie/1800342120/cast |title=The Quick and the Dead (1995) |access-date=April 10, 2011 |publisher=Yahoo! Movies |archive-date=June 24, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100624030059/http://movies.yahoo.com/movie/1800342120/cast |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Release and reception==

===Box office===
''The Quick and the Dead'' was released in the US and Canada on February 10, 1995, in 2,158 theaters, earning $6,515,861 in its opening weekend, placing second at the US box office behind ''[[Billy Madison]]'' by $124,000. The film eventually grossed $18,636,537 at the US and Canadian box office.<ref name=BoxOfficeMojo>{{cite web |url=https://www.boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=quickandthedead.htm |title=The Quick and the Dead |work=[[Box Office Mojo]] |access-date=April 10, 2011 |archive-date=August 27, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110827213336/http://boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=quickandthedead.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Writer Simon Moore noted the film performed modestly in Europe.<ref name="second" /> The movie grossed $28&nbsp;million outside the United States and Canada, for a worldwide gross of $47&nbsp;million.<ref name=SI/>

Director Sam Raimi described ''The Quick and the Dead'' as a pivotal but challenging experience. In a May 2009 interview with [[Empire (magazine)|''Empire'']] magazine, he admitted, "I had a tremendous amount to learn about directing actors", realizing he had often treated them as "props to move about". Working with stars like Gene Hackman and Sharon Stone pushed him to evolve. On his bold visual style, he reflected, "I felt my style didn't help make it into a great picture". Previously, Raimi confessed feeling lost after the film: "I was very confused. For a number of years, I thought, 'I'm like a dinosaur.' I couldn't change with the material."<ref name=second/>

TriStar Pictures also showed ''The Quick and the Dead'' as an "out-of-competition" film at the May [[1995 Cannes Film Festival]].<ref name="festival-cannes.com">{{cite web |url=http://www.festival-cannes.com/en/archives/ficheFilm/id/3381/year/1995.html |title=Festival de Cannes: The Quick and the Dead |access-date=September 8, 2009 |work=festival-cannes.com |archive-date=August 22, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110822190920/http://www.festival-cannes.com/en/archives/ficheFilm/id/3381/year/1995.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.empireonline.com/movies/features/in-conversation-sam-raimi/ | title=In Conversation with Sam Raimi | date=May 2009 |website=Empire|last=Hewitt|first=Chris}}</ref> Additionally, Stone was nominated for the [[Saturn Award for Best Actress]], but lost to [[Angela Bassett]] in ''[[Strange Days (film)|Strange Days]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.saturnawards.org/past.html |title=Past Saturn Awards |work=Academy of Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror Films |access-date=March 9, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080207072429/http://www.saturnawards.org/past.html |archive-date=February 7, 2008 }}</ref> A [[novelization]] written by [[Jack Curtis (writer)|Jack Curtis]] was published by [[HarperCollins]] in September 1995.<ref>{{cite book | title = The Quick and the Dead (Paperback) | isbn = 0006496512 | last1 = Curtis | first1 = Jack | last2 = Moore | first2 = Simon | year = 1995 | publisher = HarperCollins }}</ref> The [[DVD region code|Region 1 DVD]] was released in September 1998.<ref>{{cite book | title = The Quick and the Dead (1995) | isbn = 0767817710 }}</ref>

===Critical reception===
''The Quick and the Dead'' received mixed reviews from critics. On [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the film holds an approval rating of 62%, based on 53 reviews, with an average rating of 6.10/10. The site's consensus states: "''The Quick and the Dead'' isn't quite the draw that its intriguing premise and pedigree suggest, but fans of nontraditional Westerns should have some rootin', tootin' fun."<ref>{{cite web |title=The Quick and the Dead (1995) |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/1059629-quick_and_the_dead/ |work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |access-date=July 25, 2026 |archive-date=September 15, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200915163530/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/1059629-quick_and_the_dead |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Metacritic]] assigned the film a weighted average score of 49 out of 100, based on 21 reviews, indicating "mixed or average" reviews.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Quick and the Dead (1995): Reviews |url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/the-quick-and-the-dead/ |work=[[Metacritic]] |access-date=October 31, 2025 |archive-date=December 1, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081201120646/http://www.metacritic.com/film/titles/quickandthedead |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Janet Maslin]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' praised Stone's performance and Raimi's directing. "Stone's presence nicely underscores the genre-bending tactics of Raimi, the [[cult film]]maker now doing his best to reinvent the [[B movie]] in a spirit of self-referential glee."<ref>{{cite news | author=Maslin | title=FILM REVIEW; Sharon Stone as Taciturn Gunslinger | work=[[The New York Times]] | date=February 10, 1995|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/02/10/movies/film-review-sharon-stone-as-taciturn-gunslinger.html|page=C8|first=Janet|author-link=Janet Maslin}}</ref>

[[Roger Ebert]] of the ''[[Chicago Sun-Times]]'' criticized the film for being overtly [[cliché]]d, but praised Raimi's direction and [[Dante Spinotti]]'s [[cinematographer|cinematography]].<ref name="ebert">{{cite news | author = [[Roger Ebert]] | url = http://rogerebert.suntimes.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=/19950210/REVIEWS/502100302/1023 | title = The Quick and the Dead | work = [[Chicago Sun-Times]] | date = February 10, 1995 | access-date = March 11, 2009 | archive-date = December 1, 2008 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20081201005124/http://rogerebert.suntimes.com/apps/pbcs.dll/article?AID=%2F19950210%2FREVIEWS%2F502100302%2F1023 | url-status = dead }}</ref>

{{Quote box |quote=The cinematographer, Dante Spinotti (''[[The Last of the Mohicans (1992 film)|The Last of the Mohicans]]'') makes the material look terrific. The lowering skies around the isolated town make it look ripe for vengeance of biblical proportions, and there are quiet satirical touches, as when a man stands in a saloon door and his shadow seems about 6 miles long. |source=—Roger Ebert, writing in the ''Chicago Sun-Times''<ref name="ebert" /> |align=left |salign=left |width=40% |bgcolor=#FFFFE0}}


Critic and Raimi biographer [[Bill Warren (film historian and critic)|Bill Warren]] wrote that the film "is a very conscious (though not self-conscious) attempt to recreate some of the themes, style, and appeal of Sergio Leone's majestically operatic spaghetti Westerns of the 1960s, especially the'' [[Man with No Name]]'' trilogy that starred Clint Eastwood. It's brisker, more romantic, and somehow more American than Leone's movies."<ref name="Comp" />

[[Jonathan Rosenbaum]] of the ''[[Chicago Reader]]'' observed, "Raimi tries to do a Sergio Leone, and though ''The Quick and the Dead'' is highly enjoyable in spots, it doesn't come across as very convincing, perhaps because nothing can turn Sharon Stone into [[Charles Bronson]]."<ref>{{cite news | author=Rosenbaum | title=The Quick and the Dead | url=http://onfilm.chicagoreader.com/movies/capsules/12414_QUICK_AND_THE_DEAD | work=[[Chicago Reader]] | access-date=March 11, 2009 | archive-date=May 13, 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110513081903/http://onfilm.chicagoreader.com/movies/capsules/12414_QUICK_AND_THE_DEAD | url-status=dead |first=Jonathan|author-link=Jonathan Rosenbaum}}</ref>

[[Peter Travers]] of ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' felt that "''The Quick and the Dead'' plays like a crazed compilation of highlights from famous Westerns. Raimi finds the right look, but misses the heartbeat. You leave the film dazed instead of dazzled, as if an expert marksman had drawn his gun, only to shoot himself in the foot."<ref>{{cite magazine | author=[[Peter Travers]] | title=The Quick and the Dead | url=https://www.rollingstone.com/movies/reviews/the-quick-and-the-dead-19950101 | magazine=[[Rolling Stone]] | date=March 9, 1995 | access-date=March 10, 2011 | archive-date=January 18, 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110118230732/http://www.rollingstone.com/movies/reviews/the-quick-and-the-dead-19950101 | url-status=live }}</ref>

===Critical reassessment===
Although having a mixed critical reception on release, ''The Quick and the Dead'' has received praise from Sam Raimi fans. Tom Reimann of'' [[Valnet|Collider]]'' considers the film as one of Raimi's best movies: "The movie is so unabashedly bonkers that it’s impossible not to have a good time."<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://collider.com/box-office-bombs-that-became-classic-movies/ |title=10 Box Office Bombs That Became Classic Movies |website=[[Collider (website)|Collider]] |date=July 27, 2020 |access-date=July 27, 2020 |archive-date=July 27, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200727220901/https://collider.com/box-office-bombs-that-became-classic-movies/ |url-status=live |last=Reimann|first=Tom}}</ref>

Scott Hallam of [[Dread Central]] praised Raimi's directing and versatility in multiple genres of film and the cast.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dreadcentral.com/top-10-lists/51656/the-top-9-sam-raimi-films-horror-and-otherwise/3/|title=The Top 9 Sam Raimi Films – Horror and Otherwise|last=Hallam|first=Scott|date=February 18, 2014|work=[[Dread Central]]|access-date=October 26, 2019|archive-date=September 22, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140922060325/http://www.dreadcentral.com/top-10-lists/51656/the-top-9-sam-raimi-films-horror-and-otherwise/3/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Jay Royston of [[WhatCulture]] praised the film and considered it one of Raimi's finest movies by saying, "...I have to put it in the top three Raimi movies, maybe because it is so unlike other Raimi films, yet combines all three of the best qualities of a director already mentioned; working with actors, innovating camera shots, and telling a good story visually."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://whatculture.com/offbeat/sam-raimi-ranking-his-movies-from-worst-to-best?page=12|title=Sam Raimi: Ranking His Movies From Worst To Best|last=Royston|first=Jay|date=March 7, 2013|work=WhatCulture.com|access-date=October 26, 2019|archive-date=March 29, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190329112853/https://whatculture.com/offbeat/sam-raimi-ranking-his-movies-from-worst-to-best?page=12|url-status=live}}</ref>

Bill Gibron of ''[[PopMatters]]'' said, "This was the geek breaking point for many a certified Raimaniac. First off, it was a Western in the days when the genre was more or less struggling for life. In addition, it starred a yet to be hot Leonardo DiCaprio, a question mark named Russell Crowe, and the sexually inert Sharon Stone. About the only thing it had going for it was Raimi's manic direction, and even that seemed...showy. Still, in retrospect, this is a good film, undermined by forces outside itself."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.popmatters.com/169196-ranking-the-greats-8-the-14-films-of-sam-raimi-2495772458.html?rebelltitem=1#rebelltitem1|title=Sam Raimi: Ranking His Movies From Worst To Best|last=Gibron|first=Bill|date=March 12, 2013|work=[[PopMatters]]|access-date=October 26, 2019|archive-date=July 11, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190711152743/https://www.popmatters.com/169196-ranking-the-greats-8-the-14-films-of-sam-raimi-2495772458.html?rebelltitem=1#rebelltitem1|url-status=live}}</ref>

Matt Schimkowitz of ''[[The A.V. Club]]'' praised the film: "With a cast like that, it's expected, but it's never been this stylish, original, and fun."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.avclub.com/sam-raimi-movies-ranked-worst-to-best-1848866228/slides/11 | title=Every Sam Raimi movie, ranked from worst to best | website=[[The A.V. Club]] | date=May 5, 2022 | access-date=September 28, 2023 | archive-date=September 28, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928111942/https://www.avclub.com/sam-raimi-movies-ranked-worst-to-best-1848866228/slides/11 | url-status=live }}</ref> Ben Travis of ''[[Empire (magazine)|Empire]]'' magazine ranked it as Raimi's third-best movie: "It's a real sharp-shooter, an ultra-stylish shootout spectacular with a top cast, and some of his most creative camerawork."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.empireonline.com/movies/features/best-sam-raimi-films-ranked/ | title=Sam Raimi's 10 Best Films, Ranked | date=April 21, 2023 |website=Empire|last=Travis|first=Ben}}</ref>

Richard Schertzer of [[MovieWeb]] considered the film to be one of Raimi's best films: "With its energy, a subversive female lead from Stone, and its surprising violence, The Quick and the Dead makes for a strong entry in his repertoire as a filmmaker and a wondrous first time western for him."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://movieweb.com/best-sam-raimi-films/ | title=The Best Sam Raimi Films, Ranked | date=January 20, 2022 | access-date=May 4, 2022 | archive-date=June 28, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230628201510/https://movieweb.com/best-sam-raimi-films/ | url-status=live |website=MovieWeb|last=Schertzer|first=Richard}}</ref>

[[Patrick Phillips|Patrick Philips]] from [[Static Media|Looper]] praised the movie and considered it a "cult classic": "Of all the films on Sam Raimi's delightfully left-of-center resume, this is the one that deserves to be rediscovered by the cinematic world — if only via midnight screenings."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.looper.com/191087/every-sam-raimi-movie-ranked-worst-to-best/ | title=Every Sam Raimi Movie Ranked Worst to Best | date=February 27, 2020 | access-date=May 4, 2022 | archive-date=June 16, 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220616121130/https://www.looper.com/191087/every-sam-raimi-movie-ranked-worst-to-best/ | url-status=live |website=Looper|last=Philips|first=Patrick}}</ref> BJ Colangelo of ''[[/Film]]'' praised the movie and considered it one of Raimi's most underrated films: "There are enough dutch angle dolly zooms in this film to make someone feel disoriented, but it works. ''The Quick and the Dead'' has the heart of a classic Western, but revamped for modern audiences with snappier taste."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.slashfilm.com/848258/doctor-strange-2-director-sam-raimi-had-one-of-the-most-interesting-filmographies-of-the-90s/|title=Doctor Strange 2 Director Sam Raimi Had One Of The Most Interesting Filmographies Of The '90s |first=B. J.|last=Colangelo|date=May 3, 2022|website=[[/Film]]}}</ref>

Film critic [[Adrian Martin (film critic)|Adrian Martin]] remarked, "Sam Raimi's ''The Quick and the Dead'' is a feminist Western starring a gun-toting Sharon Stone. [There is] a terrific scene where Lady goes berserk and challenges a guy who has just sexually abused the teenage daughter of the sad saloonkeeper. Raimi takes us straight from Stone's split-second outburst of recognition to the sight of her racing forward in the pelting rain, both guns firing in righteous fury, screaming from the depths of her soul. Leone himself couldn't have done that bit any better."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.filmcritic.com.au/reviews/q/quick_and_dead.html | title=The Quick and the Dead | date=March 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190726065754/https://www.filmcritic.com.au/reviews/q/quick_and_dead.html|archive-date=July 26, 2019|url-status=usurped}}</ref>

After the release of ''[[Send Help]]'', Matt Singer of [[Townsquare Media#Assets|ScreenCrush]] ranked the film eighth of the sixteen films directed by Raimi. Singer described the film as one of the most misunderstood movies of the 1990s, calling its initial reception "their worst blunder". He praised its ensemble cast, as well as Raimi's dynamic visual style and sharp frontier dialogue, arguing the film is far deeper and more accomplished than its reputation as a shallow, melodramatic Western suggests.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Singer |first=Matt |date=2026-01-26 |title=Every Sam Raimi Movie, Ranked From Worst to Best |url=https://screencrush.com/every-sam-raimi-movie-ranked/ |access-date=2026-04-21 |website=ScreenCrush |language=en}}</ref>

[[Vulture (website)|Vulture]] ranked the film fifth among Raimi's works, describing it as a maximalist and inventive take on the Western genre, praising its exaggerated visual style, inventive camerawork, and ensemble cast, and noting that Raimi "goes for broke" in staging each duel with distinct energy and creativity.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Grebey |first=James |date=2026-01-31 |title=Every Sam Raimi Movie, Ranked |url=https://www.vulture.com/article/best-sam-raimi-movies-ranked.html |access-date=2026-04-21 |website=Vulture |language=en}}</ref>

Alison Foreman of [[IndieWire]] ranked the film among the best of Raimi’s career, placing it tenth in his filmography. She described ''The Quick and the Dead'' as a "sideways Western" elevated by its experimental visual approach and Gene Hackman's "snarling, sadistic villainy", praising its genre-blending style, horror-inflected duels, and Sharon Stone's central revenge narrative, while noting that despite its box-office disappointment, the film remains an under-appreciated entry that "packs more than expected".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Foreman |first=Alison |date=2026-02-02 |title=Sam Raimi’s 10 Best Movies, Ranked |url=https://www.indiewire.com/lists/sam-raimi-films-ranked/ |access-date=2026-04-21 |website=IndieWire |language=en-US}}</ref>
